subsection: 1. The internal structure of the earth

notes.b: The earth is not the same all the way through. It is built in layers, and each layer differs in what it is made of and whether it is solid or liquid.
points: The earth is made of concentric layers (layers one inside another, like the rings of an onion). From the outside in they are the crust, the mantle, the outer core and the inner core.
Density (how much mass is packed into a given volume) and temperature both increase towards the centre of the earth, so the innermost layers are the densest and hottest.
This is why the core, at the centre, is the hottest and densest part, while the thin crust at the surface is the coolest and lightest.
The earth's radius (the distance from the surface to the centre) is about 6,370 km.
Diagram: draw a labelled cross-section of the earth showing every layer and both boundaries between them.
notes.tip: Exams give you a labelled diagram of the earth's layers and ask you to match letters to crust, mantle, outer core and inner core. At Higher Level the diagram also includes the lithosphere, asthenosphere, oceanic crust and continental crust.

notes.b: The crust is the thin, solid outer layer of the earth, the part we live on. It exists in two types, which differ in thickness, density and rock type.
points: Continental crust (the crust that makes up the land) is about 30–70 km thick and is thickest under high mountain ranges.
Continental crust has an average density of about 2.7 g/cm³ (grams per cubic centimetre).
Continental crust is mainly granite-type rock, rich in silica (a mineral made of silicon and oxygen) and aluminium; its old name is sial.
Oceanic crust (the crust under the oceans) is about 5–10 km thick and has an average density of about 3.0 g/cm³.
Oceanic crust is mainly basalt (a dark volcanic rock), rich in silica and magnesium; its old name is sima.
Continental crust is thicker but less dense than oceanic crust, because oceanic crust is thinner but denser; compare 2.7 with 3.0 g/cm³.

No oceanic crust is older than about 200 million years, while some continental rock is billions of years old, because oceanic crust is continually created and destroyed. There is more on this in the plate tectonics model and at plate boundaries.
notes.tip: Keep the two crust types straight: continental is thicker but less dense, oceanic is thinner but denser.

notes.b: Where one layer meets the next, the rock changes sharply. These sharp boundaries have names, and exams ask you to tell them apart.
points: A discontinuity is a sharp boundary between two layers of the earth, where the material changes.
The Moho (Mohorovičić discontinuity) is the boundary between the crust and the mantle, where earthquake waves speed up suddenly.
The Moho is named after Andrija Mohorovičić, a Croatian seismologist (a scientist who studies earthquakes), who identified it in 1909 from earthquake records.
The Gutenberg discontinuity is the boundary between the mantle and the core, at the base of the mantle.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the name of the boundary between the crust and the mantle (the Moho) and what the word Moho means. The Moho separates crust and mantle; the Gutenberg discontinuity separates mantle and core. Don't swap them.

notes.b: The mantle is the thickest layer. Its upper part contains the layers on which the crust rests and moves.
points: The mantle extends to about 2,900 km depth and is made of dense rock rich in iron and magnesium.
The mantle has an upper part and a lower part, and it is the upper part that holds the asthenosphere and the base of the lithosphere.
Asthenosphere: the semi-molten (partly melted), plastic (able to flow slowly without breaking) layer in the upper mantle, beneath the lithosphere, on which the plates move. It is not liquid.
Magma is molten rock in the mantle; it is called lava only once it erupts at the surface.
Lithosphere: the rigid outer shell made of the crust plus the solid top of the upper mantle. It is about 100 km thick on average, thinner under the oceans and thicker under the continents.
The lithosphere is broken into tectonic plates (large slabs of rigid rock), which is why the rigid lithosphere can move as separate pieces over the plastic asthenosphere.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the name of the layer made of crust plus upper mantle (lithosphere), and for the name of molten rock in the mantle (magma, not lava; Ordinary Level asks this directly). Don't call the asthenosphere liquid: it is semi-molten or plastic.

notes.b: The core is the centre of the earth. It is made of iron and nickel and is divided into a liquid outer part and a solid inner part.
points: Exams ask for the two main metals of the core: iron and nickel.
Outer core: liquid, from about 2,900 km to about 5,150 km depth. Movement of this liquid metal generates the earth's magnetic field (the field that makes a compass needle point north).
Inner core: solid, from about 5,150 km to the centre of the earth. It is the hottest part of the earth, at about 5,500 °C, similar to the surface of the sun.
The inner core is solid despite its heat because the pressure at that depth is enormous, which means the metal cannot melt.
notes.tip: The outer core is liquid and the inner core is solid. Never swap them.

notes.h: Sources of heat and convection currents
notes.b: The inside of the earth is hot, and that heat keeps the mantle moving. This movement is what later drives changes in the crust.
points: Internal heat comes from the decay of radioactive elements (unstable elements that give off heat as they break down) and from heat left over from the earth's formation.
Convection currents are circular movements of semi-molten rock in the mantle, set going by heat from below, so for example hot rock rises while cooler rock sinks.
1. Heated rock near the core becomes less dense and rises.
2. Near the top of the mantle the rock spreads out sideways and cools.
3. Cooled rock becomes denser and sinks again, completing the circle.
notes.tip: Exams give a true/false statement: convection currents are circular movements of semi-molten rock in the mantle (true).

notes.b: The heat inside the earth powers forces that shape the crust. Geographers split the forces that shape the earth into those from inside and those from outside.
points: Endogenic (internal) forces come from inside the earth and are powered by its internal heat.
Endogenic forces include plate movement, folding (bending of rock layers), faulting (breaking and shifting of rock along cracks), volcanic activity and earthquakes.
Exogenic (external) forces act at the earth's surface, such as weathering (the breakdown of rock where it lies) and erosion (the wearing away and carrying off of rock and soil).
notes.tip: Exams give a true/false statement that endogenic forces act inside the earth (true), and ask for a short explanation of endogenic forces.

notes.b: Nobody has drilled through the earth, so its structure is worked out from earthquake (seismic) waves. Their speed and direction change as they pass through layers of different density.
points: Seismic waves reveal the earth's structure because the changes in their speed and direction at each boundary are how the discontinuities were found.
P-waves (primary waves) pass through both solids and liquids, so they can travel through the liquid outer core as well as through solid layers.
S-waves (secondary waves) pass only through solids, so they are stopped by any liquid layer.
S-waves do not pass through the outer core, which shows that the outer core is liquid.
This leaves an S-wave shadow zone (an area where S-waves are not detected) on the far side of the earth from an earthquake.

factCards.term: Earth's layers from the surface inward, with their depths
factCards.definition: Crust, about 5–70 km thick; mantle, to about 2,900 km; liquid outer core, from about 2,900 to 5,150 km; solid inner core, from about 5,150 km to the centre at about 6,370 km. Density and temperature increase towards the centre.

factCards.term: Continental vs oceanic crust: thickness, density and rock
factCards.definition: Continental: about 30–70 km thick, thickest under high mountains; density about 2.7 g/cm³; granite-type, rich in silica and aluminium (sial). Oceanic: about 5–10 km thick; density about 3.0 g/cm³; basalt, rich in silica and magnesium (sima).

factCards.term: Why oceanic crust is much younger than continental crust
factCards.definition: Oceanic crust is continually created and destroyed, so none is older than about 200 million years, while some continental rock is billions of years old.

factCards.term: The Moho: who identified it, when, and what happens there
factCards.definition: Andrija Mohorovičić, a Croatian seismologist, identified it in 1909 from earthquake records. At this boundary between the crust and the mantle, earthquake waves speed up suddenly.

factCards.term: Mantle: depth, rock type and the layers in its upper part
factCards.definition: The thickest layer, to about 2,900 km, of dense rock rich in iron and magnesium. Its upper part holds the semi-molten asthenosphere; its solid top joins the crust as the lithosphere, about 100 km thick on average.

factCards.term: Outer core vs inner core: state, metals and key facts
factCards.definition: Both are made of iron and nickel. The outer core is liquid, and movement of this liquid metal generates the earth's magnetic field. The inner core is solid, the hottest part of the earth at about 5,500 °C, kept solid by enormous pressure.

factCards.term: Two sources of the earth's internal heat
factCards.definition: The decay of radioactive elements, and heat left over from the earth's formation. This heat powers convection currents and endogenic forces.

factCards.term: Convection currents in the mantle: the three stages
factCards.definition: First, heated rock near the core becomes less dense and rises; then, near the top of the mantle, it spreads out sideways and cools; finally, the cooled, denser rock sinks again, completing the circle.

factCards.term: Endogenic forces: five examples, and how they differ from exogenic
factCards.definition: Plate movement, folding, faulting, volcanic activity and earthquakes. They come from inside the earth and are powered by its internal heat; exogenic forces, such as weathering and erosion, act at the surface.

factCards.term: Seismic waves: how they reveal the earth's structure
factCards.definition: Waves change speed and direction as they pass through layers of different density, which is how the discontinuities were found. P-waves pass through solids and liquids, S-waves only through solids, so S-waves failing to cross the outer core show it is liquid.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of the earth's interior.
questions.model: Crust: the thin, solid outer layer, in two types: continental crust about 30 to 70 km thick and oceanic crust about 5 to 10 km thick. Moho: the boundary between the crust and the mantle. Mantle: the thickest layer, extending to about 2,900 km depth, with the semi-molten asthenosphere in its upper part. Lithosphere: the rigid shell made of the crust plus the solid top of the upper mantle, about 100 km thick on average. Outer core: liquid, from about 2,900 km to about 5,150 km depth. Inner core: solid, from about 5,150 km to the centre of the earth.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between the lithosphere and the asthenosphere.
questions.model: The lithosphere is the rigid outer shell made of the crust plus the solid top of the upper mantle, and it is broken into plates. The asthenosphere is a semi-molten, plastic layer beneath it in the upper mantle, not a liquid, on which the plates move.

questions.prompt: Explain briefly what is meant by endogenic forces.
questions.model: Endogenic forces are internal forces that come from inside the earth and are powered by its internal heat. Examples are plate movement, folding, faulting, volcanic activity and earthquakes. They contrast with exogenic forces, which act at the surface, such as weathering and erosion.
